Shelta is a cant language, traditionally used by Irish Travelers. It is characterized by its use of both Irish and English words, as well as a large number of unique Shelta words. One such word is "/ꭕ/", a hissing sound held in the back of the throat, which can be found in the word "skraꭕo" meaning 'tree, bush'.

Loanwords from Shelta have made their way into mainstream English, such as the word "bloke" meaning 'a man', which was borrowed in the mid-19th century.

The orthography of Shelta is not standardized and can be written using either an Irish-type or English-type orthography. For example, the word for 'married' can be spelled "lósped" or "lohsped", and the word for 'woman' can be spelled "beoir" or "byohr".

For comparison, here are reproductions of the Lord's Prayer in Shelta as it occurred a century ago, current Shelta Cant, and modern English and Irish versions:

Shelta (circa 1900):
Athera thi, art in heaben;
Thy hole name be hallowed;
Thy ken come;
Thy will be done, in erv as it is in heaben;
Give us this day our chore loaf;
And forgive us our sins, as we forgive them that sins agin us;
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

Shelta Cant (current):
Our Father who art in heaven,
Hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come.
Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us this day our daily bread,
And forgive us our debts,
As we also have forgiven our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation,
But deliver us from evil.
